title: The captive girl (2 Kings 5:2–3)
hook: an Israelite servant girl points her master toward healing

segments.voice: Yesterday, a great general almost refused the plain instruction: wash, and be clean. Did you try the simple thing? Today we go back to the start of that story, to the person who sent him to the prophet at all. Day seven hundred seventy-four.

She gets only a few lines. No name, no age, no words about her family. Raiding bands from Aram had gone into the land of Israel, and among what they carried off was a young girl. Now she works in a foreign house, waiting on the wife of the commander of the army whose raiders took her. That commander is Naaman. Everything we heard yesterday, the chariots, the gifts, the journey to Elisha's door, the river, begins with something this girl says to her mistress.
screen: `A FEW LINES, NO NAME.` → `CARRIED OFF BY RAIDERS.` → `SERVING IN NAAMAN'S HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Here is what she says, in the King James words: "Would God my lord were with the prophet that is in Samaria! for he would recover him of his leprosy." Read that slowly and look at who she's talking about. My lord. The man whose soldiers took her from her home. And her wish is for him to be healed. The text doesn't tell us what she felt. It doesn't say whether she was afraid, or homesick, or angry. It doesn't explain her motives at all. It only gives us the sentence, and the sentence is generous. Then notice how far that sentence travels. Word of it goes up the household: thus and thus said the maid from the land of Israel. It reaches the king of Aram, and he writes a letter to the king of Israel. Armies and kings and letters start moving, all because a servant girl spoke up. The next verses say the king of Israel panics when he reads the letter, tearing his clothes and asking, am I God, to kill and to make alive? The king doesn't think of the prophet. The girl did. She knew there was a prophet in Samaria, and she trusted he could help. Two more things stand out. First, she points away from herself. She doesn't claim any power. She simply knows where help can be found. Second, the story never mentions her again. No reward, no freedom, no thanks recorded. Naaman comes home healed, and the text has already moved on. But the healing began with her one sentence. It came from someone with no power at all, and the text bothered to keep it.
screen: `WOULD GOD MY LORD WERE WITH THE PROPHET.` · `THE SENTENCE TRAVELS TO KINGS.` · then, large: `A SMALL GIRL'S WORD.` · then: `NEVER MENTIONED AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be kind to someone who wronged you. This one is hard, so go gently. Sit still for a moment. Think of someone who hurt you in a small or middle-sized way. Not the deepest wound; something you can hold for two minutes. You don't have to excuse what they did. Just ask the girl's question: is there one good thing I could wish for this person? Healing, rest, a better day. Let that wish sit for a few breaths. If it won't come, that's honest too; simply notice it. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayers. The bell holds the time.
The captive girl. A young Israelite taken by raiders, serving in Naaman's house, whose one sentence sent her master to be healed. Today's word.
Your line: a small girl's word. Today, wish one person who wronged you something good, even quietly, and see if a kind word can find its way out. Day seven hundred seventy-four.

howItsDone: Jews read the captive girl's words at the start of Naaman's story in the book of Kings, which is read in synagogue as a haftarah.

fork.setup: you're a servant taken from your home. your master, the man whose army took you, is sick. what does the girl do?
options: stay silent; it's not her concern.
tell her mistress about the prophet who could heal him.
ask for her freedom in exchange for help.
fork.reveal: she says, would God my lord were with the prophet that is in Samaria! she asks nothing for herself.

original.note: Hebrew: a little maid, the text's description of her in 2 Kings 5:2.

trapdoor: what you thought: a side character in Naaman's story.
what it means: a captive with no power wishes healing on her captor, and her word sets kings in motion.
what a scholar hears: she is a na'arah ketanah, a little girl, beside Naaman the great man; healed, his flesh is like a little boy's.

notes: Auditor (2026-10-01): practice opening varied; trapdoor floor now the na'arah ketanah (5:2) / ish gadol (5:1) / na'ar katan (5:14) contrast; Keeper verify Hebrew.

Editor: dropped the 'two verses' count and the 'only description' superlative; 5:4 is ambiguous about who told whom, so the relay is now 'word reaches the king'; 'the very commander whose army took her' softened to his army's raiders; cut invented kitchen/hallway setting and a doubled 'turns on' sentence.
Verify KJV wording at 2 Kings 5:3; JPS 1917 differs ('Would that my lord were...') and a Keeper may prefer it.
The script avoids giving the girl an age, feelings or motive; it says plainly the text is silent.
'Two verses' refers to 5:2–3, the only verses that describe her directly (her words are retold in 5:4).
The king of Israel's reaction (5:7) is paraphrased.
The practice asks for kindness to someone who wronged you; it is framed gently and avoids severe harm; Keeper may wish to add a note on forgiveness in Jewish thought.
